# Boats and Boatbuilding

*Pages PDF 92-102*

## **Boats and Boatbuilding**
# **The Basics of Putting a Boat Together and Outfitting a Vessel**
Just like Characters, boats have Characteristics that describe their abilities. They can also have Traits to give them specific capabilities. Described below are the stats for boats typical of their type. Any two boats, however, are rarely alike; their Characteristics vary with their states of repair, workmanship, lay-out, and design. A boat’s profile is laid out as follows: 

|**Boat**|**Name**|**Cost**|**Crew**|**Sail**<br>**M (C)**|**Oars**<br>**M (C)**|**Man**|**Size**|**T**|**W**|**Carries**|**Traits and**<br>**Upgrades**|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## **Boat Name**
This is the name of the vessel or, if its individual name is unknown or unimportant, the general scale or design of the vessel. 

## **Cost**
This figure is an indication of the cost of a brand-new boat straight out of the shipyard. 

## **Crew**
This figure is an indication of the number of crew that the boat can comfortably carry and that will normally be expected of such a vessel. If more crew or passengers board the ship they will have to be counted against the Carries Characteristic of the ship. 

A member of the crew also takes up more Crew spaces or Carries space depending on their Size. The following numbers are a rough guide to how much space a Character takes up on a boat: 

||**CREW BULK**<br>**Size**<br>**Crew Spaces Taken Up**<br>**Enc**<br>Tiny<br>–<br>–<br>Little<br>0.25<br>1<br>Small<br>0.5<br>3<br>Average<br>1<br>6<br>Large<br>3<br>18<br>Enormous<br>9<br>54<br>Monstrous<br>27<br>162|
|---|---|

Items worn or carried by a Character do not count against the space or weight limits of a boat unless they are very bulky and weighty. Unless an item is as bulky as a small crate of cargo (1 foot cubed) it is considered irrelevant in terms of working out whether the boat is Encumbered. However, it is up to the GM to consider where to draw the lines. A couple of Characters dressed in full plate armour are unlikely to make a great deal of difference — but equipping a large crew with full plate armour ought to count. A few Tiny creatures do not add to Crew or Enc, but dozens should. 

## **Sail M (C)**
This Characteristic is split into two numbers. The first number (M) is the boat’s Movement, assuming that the minimum number of crew are available, the conditions are fair, and no attempt is being made to push the boat to go faster. 

The second number (C) is the minimum number of crew required to sail the vessel at its Movement for a relatively short stretch of rigorous sailing, such as an eight-hour shift. For longer stretches, larger crews may be required. 

## **Oars M (C)**
As with Sail, the first number (M) is the boat’s Movement score, assuming that the minimum number of crew are available, the conditions are fair, and rowing is taking place at a moderate pace. The second number (C) is the minimum number of crew required to row the vessel at its Movement for a two-hour stretch. 

## **Manoeuvre (Man)**
The Manoeuvre Characteristic provides a modifier to be imposed on Tests where the responsiveness and agility of the vessel is important. These include Sail Tests and Row Tests in areas where there are hazards, but other Tests may be affected. 

## **Size**
An indication of a vessel’s length in yards. Size influences a ship’s speed and determines its Carries Characteristic. 

## **Toughness (T)**
The Toughness of a ship is used to test whether it can withstand Damage. The first digit of the boat’s Toughness is also used as the Toughness Bonus (TB). The TB of a ship is subtracted from any Damage done to it, before applying this to the Wounds. 

## **Wounds (W)**
Like a Character’s Wounds, the Wounds Characteristic for a ship is a measure of how much Damage it can take. 

## **Carries**
This is the Encumbrance value of the cargo that the ship can comfortably carry. A ship loaded with more cargo suffers penalties to speed and manoeuvrability. 

||**Degree of Additional**<br>**Encumbrance**<br>**Effect on Vessel**<br>More than Carries<br>–1 M, –1 SL Manoeuvre<br>20% more than Carries<br>–2 M, –2 SL Manoeuvre<br>40% more than Carries<br>–3 M, –3 SL Manoeuvre<br>50% more than Carries<br>Not seaworthy|
|---|---|

Personal items worn or carried by members of the crew will not normally count against the Carries capacity. 

The amount of Wounds a boat has remaining is important for working out its ability to withstand collisions and other forms of damage. The first digit of the boat’s Wounds is also used as the Wounds Bonus (WB). This is worked out according to a ship’s current Wounds, so may change during an encounter. 

## **Traits and Upgrades**
Traits and Upgrades are design features that can be applied to a vessel. Traits are integral to the craft and are implemented as the vessel is built, whereas Upgrades can be added or removed later. Traits and Upgrades are described on page 97.

## XII
## **Building a Boat**
This section can be used as a guide for players to commission and build their own vessels, or to give the GM a way to create boats. To determine the cost of a new boat, the prospective owner must decide on several factors: the boat’s size; how it is propelled; whether its design affects manoeuvrability, speed, or cargo space; and whether the ship has any Traits or Upgrades applied to it. 

An owner also has the option to add several Upgrades to the vessel, though these could be added at a later date if it would be more convenient. 

## **Step 1 – Size**
To start, you must select a Size or type of boat. This gives base Characteristics which can then be adjusted by design choices. You start with the typical boat Characteristics given above, and modify those, or begin from scratch using the **Generic Boat Characteristics** table. 

Note that some of the example boats cannot be made exactly with the ship building rules below, but that is testament to the many shipbuilders across the Sea of Claws and the varied techniques they employ. Use the table below as a rough guide. The listed price is for a boat of the indicated size with no modifiers or extras.

## **Step 2 – Choose Primary Propulsion: Sails or Oars**
Many ships have a Sail Characteristic and an Oar one, but they always rely on one over the other — the Longship is designed for rowing and makes a relatively poor sailing vessel; the Wolfship is designed for sailing on the high seas, but it is fitted with oars in case winds are low or blowing from an inconvenient direction. Choose which method of propulsion is the main method and reduce the Movement of the other by 2 to a minimum of 3. Note that the largest ships cannot be propelled by oars. 

**Step 3 – Adjust Cost According to Manoeuvrability** Poor manufacture, cheap materials, or fundamental flaws with the design can result in the vessel making manoeuvres at a penalty. While excellent design can bring a bonus, it comes at a cost. Ships have been refined through trial and error over hundreds of years, so creating a ship with a manoeuvre bonus involves painstaking practices and the finest materials.

|<br>–2 SL|<br>–40%|
|–1 SL|–20%|
|+1 SL|+20%|

## **Step 4 – Adjust Cost According to Speed**
The speed of the ship is derived from the M value of its Sails or Oars and adjusted using the table below. Any increase in speed is limited by cargo space, so the Carries Characteristic is adjusted according to the ship’s speed. Extremely fast ships cost more. ## **Traits**
The following Traits can be built into a ship. Unlike Upgrades, these cannot be added or adjusted once the frame is complete. 

## **Armoured**
This boat is built for fighting, with reinforcements and wooden and metal plates added at strategic locations. Each level of this Trait adds 10 to the Toughness of a vessel. Ships can have up to 3 levels of Armoured. 

- Subtract 10% of the base Carries and add 10% to the base Cost per level of _Armoured_ . 

## **Rugged**
Rugged ships are generally unspectacular but well-made. They are tried and tested designs that have proved themselves on the high seas in the worst weather. Anything that is likely _Rugged_ ship gets +2 to fall off will have fallen off by now. A SL to Batten Down the Hatches Crew Tests (see page 123). 

Add 10% of the base Cost. 

## **Sturdy**
_Sturdy_ ships are built to withstand the rigours of war. Boats can have up to three levels of _Sturdy_ , and each level increases the Wounds of a vessel by 30%. 

- Subtract 10% of the base Carries and add 20% to the base Cost for each level of Sturdy. 

## **Unwieldy**
Utilitarian boats intended to work close to shore or on calm seas are cobbled together by amateur shipwrights, or commissioned by owners looking to scrimp on the cost. The poorly designed craft can take up to 3 levels of the _Unwieldy_ Trait to represent their design flaws. Each level imposes a penalty of –1 SL to any Sail Tests or Row Tests. 

- Subtract 10% of the base Cost per level of Unwieldy. 

## **Upgrades**
There are many ways to modify a craft if one has the money. Several Upgrades are provided in the **Death on the Reik Companion** . However, **Sea of Claws** deals with ship movement and interaction on a larger scale than the River Travel rules in that book, so not all Upgrades given in the **Death on the Reik Companion** are relevant. 

The Upgrades listed here are those that are pertinent to ocean-going vessels and warships. 

## **Size and Upgrades**
Note that Tiny and Little vessels tend to be too small or short to fit many of these Upgrades. 

## **Anchor**
**Cost:** 10 GC (for boats of Size Small to Average), 20 GC (for larger boats). 

**Weight:** 50 Encumbrance points (for boats of Size Tiny to Average), 75 Encumbrance points (for bigger boats). 

A ship without an Anchor has no way to fix itself in place when at sea. A ship that deploys its Anchor in a suitable location (many parts of the ocean are too deep) is not affected by winds or currents whilst the anchor is lowered. 

Raising an Anchor is not an easy process. If an Anchor needs to be raised in a hurry the crew must work hard at the capstan; an **Extended Strength** Test is required to raise the Anchor. The difficulty of the Test depends on the Size of the ship (typically it will be **Difficult (–10)** for Small or Average ships and **Hard (–20)** for bigger boats), and the total SL needed depend on the depth of the Anchor (a typical value would be 15 SL). 

## **Armour Plating**
**Cost:** 250 GC (Bronze) or 330 GC (Iron) per 5 yards of Size for Small to Average ships; 500 GC (Bronze) or 560 GC (Iron) per 5 yards of Size for larger ships. 

**Weight (per 5 yards of Size):** +160 Encumbrance points (Iron); +175 Encumbrance points (Bronze). 

Armour Plating may only be added at specialised shipyards, and involves the skills of expert smiths as well as shipwrights. Adding the armour takes two weeks for Tiny to Average ships, and a month for larger ships. 

Armour on a vessel works in much the same way as armour on a character. The Damage of hits to the Hull is reduced by the AP as well as the TB. Unlike personal armour, ship armour may not be sacrificed to avoid Critical Wounds. 

**Bronze:** The Hull benefits from 1 AP. 

**Iron:** The Hull benefits from 2 AP; if the vessel becomes Fouled (see page 105) the iron plates rust to the point of uselessness, losing all armour value. 

## **Crow’s Nest**
**Cost:** 5 GC (Small to Average boats), 20 GC (Large to Monstrous boats). 

**Weight:** 5 Encumbrance points (Small to Average boats), 20 Encumbrance points (Large to Monstrous boats). 

A Crow’s Nest is a wooden platform placed atop the tallest mast. A Character in the Crow’s Nest may take any Perception Tests called for to spot visible phenomena at sea, such as hazards, or the light from lighthouses. The Crow’s Nest provides benefits to Perception Tests depending on the ship’s Size: +1 SL (Tiny to Average boats), +2 SL (Large to Monstrous boats).

## **Gun Ports**
**Cost:** 15 GC (for boats of Size Tiny to Average), 85 GC (for larger boats). 

**Cost:** 2 GC. 

**Weight:** +0 Encumbrance points. 

**Weight:** 10 Encumbrance points. 

Figureheads are brightly painted wooden sculptures attached to the front of a boat. They are thought to attract luck and help personalise the ship, as well as helping to show that the owner possesses wit and humanity. Most Figureheads depict aspects of Manann, a mermaid, or a romanticised personification of the owner’s heraldry or nationality. 

If the Figurehead is particularly well made it becomes a source of pride for the crew. A Figurehead with two or more _Fine_ Qualities adds 1 to the Morale total (see page 124). 

## **Flying Ib J**
**Cost:** 5 GC (Tiny boats), 20 GC (Little boats), 40 GC (Small boats), 80 GC (Average boats), 160 GC (Large boats), 320 GC (Enormous boats), 600 GC (Monstrous boats). 

**Weight:** 5 Encumbrance points (Tiny boats), 25 Encumbrance points (Little boats), 45 Encumbrance points (Small boats), 70 Encumbrance points (Average boats), 135 Encumbrance points (Large boats), 240 Encumbrance points (Enormous boats), 430 Encumbrance points (Monstrous boats). 

Gun Ports are closable hatches that allow a missile weapon to be fired from behind cover. Large Gun Ports can accommodate cannon or ballistae, while small Gun Ports are intended for handguns, bows, and crossbows. 

If a ship has no Gun Ports, any shooting must be performed from the deck. The deck provides no cover, whilst a Gun Port provides Hard Cover. Opening or closing a Gun Port counts as a single action. Open Gun Ports can prove a liability if the ship begins to sink (see page 117). 

## **Luxury Cabins**
**Cost:** 155 GC per cabin. 

**Weight:** 40 Encumbrance points per cabin. 

Taking the space of two normal cabins, a Luxury Cabin allows the occupant to journey in comfort and style. At the GM’s discretion, any Fellowship Tests made by the owner of a Luxury Cabin gain a +10 bonus, provided they are made within the cabin. 

## **’ Ship S Boat**
**Cost:** As per the design of the Ship’s Boat. 

A Flying Jib is an extra foresail that requires a bowsprit to be added. Larger boats have more complex arrangements of multiple sails that perform the same function. Adding a bowsprit increases a vessel’s length by 10%. 

A sailing ship with a Flying Jib uses the following Wind Effect table rather than the one provided on page 107. 

**Weight:** As per the design of the Ship’s Boat. 

If a ship has a sufficient Carries capacity, it may carry another boat. This could be used to ferry cargo or passengers between the main ship and port, as a life raft in an emergency, or even to tow the larger boat (at M1 and Man –4 SL). 

## **Ram**
**Cost:** 15 GC (Tiny and Little boats), 30 GC (Small and Average boats), 60 GC (Large boats), 120 GC (Enormous boats), 240 GC (Monstrous boats). 

**Weight:** 30 Encumbrance points (Tiny and Little boats), 60 Encumbrance points (Small and Average boats), 120 Encumbrance points (Large boats), 240 Encumbrance points (Enormous boats), 480 Encumbrance points (Monstrous boats). 

A metal Ram can be fitted to the front of a boat. The Ram provides the ship with 5 AP that can protect from any Damage resulting from a collision or attack coming from the front of the vessel. The ship also adds 5 to its Toughness Bonus when calculating its Collision Rating (see page 111) if it is the vessel causing the collision and strikes head on. 

## **Smoothing**
**Cost:** 66 GC per 5 yards of Size for Tiny to Average ships; and 132 GC per 5 yards of Size for larger ships. 

## **Weight:** None.
The boat’s hull is smoothed to remove any irregularities that might cause unnecessary drag. Initial Smoothing of a hull takes one week at a boatyard for Tiny to Average ships, and two weeks for larger ships. A smooth hull gives the boat M +1. 

Repairing a smoothed hull costs 50% more than normal (see page 116). Cheaper repairs lose the benefits of the Smoothing. 

## **Water Brakes**
**Cost:** 10 GC (Tiny boats), 45 GC (Little boats), 75 GC (Small boats), 140 GC (Average boats), 200 GC (Large boats), 350 GC (Enormous boats), 500 GC (Monstrous boats). 

**Weight:** 15 Encumbrance points (Tiny boats), 40 Encumbrance points (Little boats), 50 Encumbrance points (Small boats), 110 Encumbrance points (Average boats), 150 Encumbrance points (Large boats), 300 Encumbrance points (Enormous boats), 550 Encumbrance points (Monstrous boats). 

This apparatus consists of two broad wooden flaps that can be unfolded from the sides of the boat. When moving forwards, opening the brakes increases drag and reduces Movement by 1 or 2 points, depending on whether they are opened halfway or fully. If deployed whilst in a strait or whirlpool, they increase the effective M of the current by a similar amount. 

## **Steam Engine**
**Cost:** 500 GC 

## **Weight:** 200 Encumbrance Points
A boat powered by a steam engine has an M of 4 for as long as the fuel holds out, regardless of wind direction. It requires tending by a qualified engineer, with Trade (Engineer) Tests made for Boat Handling Tests.

## **Artillery Pieces**
Sailing is fraught with danger, and even small trading vessels tend to mount serious weaponry. In the right hands, a few small cannon can make a Bretonnian privateer or Norse raiding party search for easier pickings. 

**Note:** Artillery pieces must use special ammunition as detailed in the table below. Despite being a Blackpowder weapon, a Cannon may not fire bullets designed for a Handgun, and a Ballista may not shoot Crossbow bolts. 

The weapons listed here are a selection of those that could be fitted to a vessel. For more information on artillery, see **Up in Arms** . However, this selection does represent those weapons commonly found on ships of the Empire. 

Artillery pieces follow principles developed for smaller weapons. Marines with working knowledge of a crossbow can load and fire ballistae, and cannons are no more intricate than handguns. However, most siege weapons do require a crew to shoot with acceptable degrees of accuracy or rate of fire. 

As with handheld ranged weapons, it is not normally possible to operate a siege weapon without training in the relevant weapon group. A person with **Ranged (Crossbow)** could not crew a Cannon, but those with **Ranged (Engineering** ) can crew Blackpowder weapons with no penalty. 

## **Ballistae**
Ballistae are large, torsion-powered crossbows. They shoot iron-capped bolts much heavier than those fired from regular crossbows. These bolts are powerful enough to impale sailors or punch neat holes through the hull. 

## **Cannons**
The cannons of the Empire are precision engineered weapons produced in great quantity in the nation’s cities, most famously that of Nuln. 

## **Mortars**
A Mortar fires a heavy ball or bomb in a high arc. On the battlefield, they are used mainly in sieges, throwing explosives over castle walls. Whilst they are not as effective at smashing through hulls as cannon fire, they can be deadly to crew on deck and help spread fire on an enemy vessel. 

Ballistae are relatively simple to use. Any Character can attempt a **Ranged (Crossbow)** Test using their BS, but the weapon loses all Qualities whilst retaining its Flaws. 

## **Swivel Guns**
A Swivel Gun is like a blunderbuss, but larger. Because of its weight, it is normally mounted on a swivel or tripod.

## **Placing Cannon on Deck**
The owner of the boat should be allowed to decide how to place cannon (and other heavy items) on board their vessel. Some may like to arrange all their guns on one side of the ship in order to unleash a devastating broadside, or cram them in around the prow in order to blast apart enemies as they close. Whilst this might provide tactical advantages in combat, it does compromise the ship’s ability to move and manoeuvre. 

- If the weight of the guns on one facing of the ship exceeds 25% of the ship’s Carries capacity, the ship suffers an additional –1 to its M and Man, and Boat Handling Tests suffer from –1 SL. 

- If the weight of the guns on one facing of the ship exceeds 50% of the ship’s Carries capacity, the ship suffers an additional –2 to its M and Man, and Boat Handling Tests suffer from –2 SL. 

The diagram to the right shows four ways ten cannon could be arranged on deck. The top two placements are sensible and would not impose penalties on the handling of the vessel. The bottom two placements will impose penalties unless compensatory ballast, such as sandbags, is placed to make the weight distribution more even. 

## **New Weapon Qualities and Flaws**
## **Crewed**
A weapon with the Crewed Flaw is so large, heavy, and complex that it benefits from being managed by a team rather than a single operator. Everyone on this team needs to possess the relevant Ranged Skill to crew the weapon. However, they may nominate one of their number to make the relevant Ranged Test to see how well the weapon performs when it is triggered. 

Most weapons have a crew of 2, 3, or 4. Larger crews are often assembled, but extraneous crew members do not impact the efficiency of the weapon itself, though they may help move it or make up for casualties in the thick of battle. 

If a weapon requiring a crew is not fully crewed it is impaired as explained in the table below. 

||**Crew**<br>**Crewed 2**<br>**Crewed 3**<br>**Crewed 4**<br>4<br>N/A<br>N/A<br>N/A<br>3<br>N/A<br>N/A<br>Double Reload<br>Time<br>2<br>N/A<br>Double<br>Reload Time<br>Gain_Imprecise_<br>Flaw<br>1<br>Double<br>Reload<br>Time<br>Gain_Imprecise_<br>Flaw<br>Gain_Dangerous_<br>Flaw|
|---|---|

If a weapon gains a Flaw that it already possesses, impose a further penalty of –10 to any Ranged Tests made to shoot the weapon. 

When reloading a weapon with the _Crewed_ Flaw, one of the crew may assist with any Tests made to determine how long the reloading process takes. 

If a weapon with the _Crewed_ Flaw suffers a misfire, all members of the crew are affected. 

## **Spread (Rating)**
Weapons with the Spread Quality fire an expanding cloud of projectiles which may strike several targets. Depending on the range to the target, weapons with this Quality behave somewhat differently. 

- **Point Blank:** The shot targets a single individual. Add (Rating) to the weapon’s Damage. 

- **Short Range to Long Range:** The shot targets a single individual, and also the next (Rating) closest visible creatures. No two targets may be more than (Rating) yards apart. 

- **Extreme Range:** As for Short to Long Range but reduce the weapon’s Damage by (Rating). 

Penalties from reduced crew are cumulative, so a Crewed 4 weapon with a single crewman will suffer from double reload time, the _Imprecise_ Flaw, and the _Dangerous_ Flaw.
